scores.reason: Consumer, self-directed fintech field experiment showing a choice-architecture change shifts nominal enrolment behavior without changing the financial outcome — directly tests the brief's central 'vanity metric' worry (C2, C4).

Pre-checked recurring micro-contribution default with causal effect size, regret (refunds), and heterogeneity concentrated on small/inexperienced users — hits C1 and C5 and maps closely onto round-up enrolment and dark-pattern risk, despite the donation domain.

The contradicting-the-premise paper the brief explicitly asked for: shows the default effect on actual savings largely erodes at steady state once attrition and opt-out are modeled, with effect sizes — squarely C1 and C2, employer setting acknowledged as the closest analogous literature.

At-scale automatic enrolment into a discretionary consumer-bank feature with real effect sizes (C1, C4), but the feature is alerts rather than a contribution decision, so it informs the entry choice only by analogy.

Directly answers the level-design question (C3): shows preset menus anchor via friction rather than preference, and quantifies the welfare effect of adding a lower preset option — precisely the 1×/2×/5× multiplier decision, in a consumer self-directed setting.

Review of when default effects persist versus fade downstream — genuinely useful for the 6–12 month measurement question (C2), though it offers a framework and agenda rather than the effect sizes the brief asked a review to supply.

European consumer samples showing defaults move behavior with medium-large effect sizes while damaging trust when refused, plus framing/anchoring effects — directly informs the helpful-vs-manipulative question the brief flags under EU scrutiny (C1, C3, C5).

A bibliometric-style mapping of the nudge literature with no effect sizes or default-specific findings; shares the domain but would not change either the entry or level decision — not the effect-size review the brief requested.

Foundational slot: the canonical synthesis of household-finance behavior and choice-architecture interventions across consumer contexts — the background the newer papers on this list are refining, and what a newcomer should read first.

Foundational slot: well-known evidence that a well-intentioned nudge in a consumer financial app harms a vulnerable subgroup while helping the average — real background for the brief's distributional worry, though it concerns reminders rather than defaults and is not the one canonical default paper.
